rows.stem: The direction ratios of a line parallel to z-axis are :
rows.solution: A line parallel to the z-axis points along \(\hat{k}\), so a vector along it is \(0\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 1\hat{k}\) and its direction ratios are \(\langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle\). Equivalently, such a line makes an angle of \(90^\circ\) with both the x-axis and the y-axis and \(0^\circ\) with the z-axis, so its direction cosines are \(0, 0, 1\). Note that \(\langle 0, 0, 0 \rangle\) can never be a set of direction ratios, since a direction requires a non-zero vector. So the direction ratios are \(\langle 0, 0, 1 \rangle\).

rows.stem: Ashima can hit a target 2 out of 3 times. She tried to hit the target twice. The probability that she missed the target exactly once is
rows.solution: Hitting the target 2 out of 3 times means \(P(\text{hit}) = \frac{2}{3}\), so \(P(\text{miss}) = 1 - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}\). The two attempts are independent. Missing exactly once can happen in two ways — miss then hit, or hit then miss — each of probability \(\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{2}{9}\). Hence the required probability is \(2 \times \frac{2}{9} = \frac{4}{9}\). (Equivalently, by the binomial law with \(n = 2\), \(\binom{2}{1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^1\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^1 = \frac{4}{9}\).) So the probability is \(\frac{4}{9}\).

options.label: A
options.text: continuous but not differentiable at x = 0.

options.label: C
options.text: neither continuous nor differentiable at x = 0.

options.label: D
options.text: differentiable but not continuous at x = 0.

rows.solution: Write the function without the modulus: for \(x \ge 0\), \(|x| = x\) so \(f(x) = x - x = 0\); for \(x < 0\), \(|x| = -x\) so \(f(x) = -x - x = -2x\). For continuity at \(x = 0\): \(\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^-}(-2x) = 0\), \(\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = 0\), and \(f(0) = 0\), so all three agree and \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\). For differentiability at \(x = 0\), compare the one-sided derivatives: the left-hand derivative is \(\lim_{h \to 0^-}\frac{f(h) - f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-}\frac{-2h}{h} = -2\), while the right-hand derivative is \(\lim_{h \to 0^+}\frac{0 - 0}{h} = 0\). Since \(-2 \ne 0\), \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = 0\). Hence the function is continuous but not differentiable at \(x = 0\).

rows.stem: If \(\begin{bmatrix} x & 2 \\ 3 & x - 1 \end{bmatrix}\) is a singular matrix, then the product of all possible values of x is :
rows.solution: A matrix is singular when its determinant is zero. Here \(\begin{vmatrix} x & 2 \\ 3 & x - 1 \end{vmatrix} = x(x - 1) - (2)(3) = x^2 - x - 6\). Setting this to zero, \(x^2 - x - 6 = 0\), i.e. \((x - 3)(x + 2) = 0\), so the possible values are \(x = 3\) and \(x = -2\). Their product is \(3 \times (-2) = -6\). (One may read this off the quadratic directly: the product of the roots of \(x^2 - x - 6 = 0\) is \(\frac{c}{a} = -6\).) So the product of all possible values is \(-6\).

A primitive is an antiderivative, so we must integrate. Use the double-angle identity \(\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1\), which gives \(1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x\). Hence the expression simplifies to \(\frac{2}{1 + \cos 2x} = \frac{2}{2\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x\), and its primitive is \(\int \sec^2 x\,dx = \tan x + C\). Note that \(\sec^2 x\) is the simplified integrand itself, not its primitive. So the primitive is \(\tan x\).

rows.stem: For what value of \(\lambda\), the projection of vector \(\hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j}\) on vector \(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\) is \(\sqrt{2}\) ?
rows.solution: The projection of \(\vec{a}\) on \(\vec{b}\) is \(\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}\). With \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \lambda\hat{j}\) and \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}\), the dot product is \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = (1)(1) + (\lambda)(-1) = 1 - \lambda\), and \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{1^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{2}\). Setting the projection equal to \(\sqrt{2}\): \(\frac{1 - \lambda}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\), so \(1 - \lambda = 2\) and \(\lambda = -1\). So the value is \(-1\).

rows.stem: If the product of two positive numbers is 9, find the numbers so that the sum of their squares is minimum.
rows.solution: Let the two positive numbers be \(x\) and \(\frac{9}{x}\), so that their product is \(9\). The quantity to minimise is the sum of their squares, \(f(x) = x^2 + \left(\frac{9}{x}\right)^2 = x^2 + \frac{81}{x^2}\), for \(x > 0\). Differentiating, \(f'(x) = 2x - \frac{162}{x^3}\). Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) gives \(2x = \frac{162}{x^3}\), so \(2x^4 = 162\), \(x^4 = 81\) and hence \(x = 3\), taking the positive root since the numbers are positive. To confirm this is a minimum, \(f''(x) = 2 + \frac{486}{x^4}\), which is positive for every \(x > 0\), so \(f\) is minimum at \(x = 3\). The other number is \(\frac{9}{3} = 3\). Hence both numbers are \(3\), and the least sum of squares is \(3^2 + 3^2 = 18\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Form
rows.stem: If \(x = \sqrt{a^{\tan^{-1} t}}\), \(y = \sqrt{a^{\cot^{-1} t}}\), then show that \(x \frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0\).
rows.solution: Write each variable as a power of \(a\): \(x = \sqrt{a^{\tan^{-1} t}} = a^{\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} t}\) and \(y = \sqrt{a^{\cot^{-1} t}} = a^{\frac{1}{2}\cot^{-1} t}\). Differentiating with respect to the parameter \(t\), and using \(\frac{d}{dt}\tan^{-1} t = \frac{1}{1 + t^2}\), \(\frac{d}{dt}\cot^{-1} t = -\frac{1}{1 + t^2}\): \(\frac{dx}{dt} = a^{\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1} t}\log a \cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{1 + t^2} = \frac{x\log a}{2(1 + t^2)}\), and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = a^{\frac{1}{2}\cot^{-1} t}\log a \cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{1 + t^2}\right) = -\frac{y\log a}{2(1 + t^2)}\). Dividing, every common factor cancels: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = -\frac{y}{x}\). Multiplying by \(x\) gives \(x\frac{dy}{dx} = -y\), that is \(x\frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0\), as required.

The integrand is even in \(x\) with only \(x^2\) appearing, so substitute \(t = x^2\) in the partial-fraction step alone: \(\frac{t}{(t + 4)(t + 9)} = \frac{A}{t + 4} + \frac{B}{t + 9}\) gives \(t = A(t + 9) + B(t + 4)\). Putting \(t = -4\): \(-4 = 5A\), so \(A = -\frac{4}{5}\); putting \(t = -9\): \(-9 = -5B\), so \(B = \frac{9}{5}\). Restoring \(t = x^2\), \(\frac{x^2}{(x^2 + 4)(x^2 + 9)} = -\frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{x^2 + 4} + \frac{9}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{x^2 + 9}\). Now integrate each term with \(\int\frac{dx}{x^2 + a^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + C\): \(\int\frac{x^2\,dx}{(x^2 + 4)(x^2 + 9)} = -\frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{2} + \frac{9}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{3}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{3} + C = -\frac{2}{5}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{2} + \frac{3}{5}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{3} + C\).

rows.stem:
Find the general solution of the differential equation :
\(\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{2y}{x} = \sin \frac{1}{x}\).
rows.solution: The equation is linear in \(y\), of the form \(\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\) with \(P = -\frac{2}{x}\) and \(Q = \sin\frac{1}{x}\). The integrating factor is \(e^{\int -\frac{2}{x}\,dx} = e^{-2\log x} = \frac{1}{x^2}\). Multiplying through, the solution is \(y\cdot\frac{1}{x^2} = \int \frac{1}{x^2}\sin\frac{1}{x}\,dx + C\). For that integral put \(t = \frac{1}{x}\), so \(dt = -\frac{1}{x^2}dx\) and \(\int \frac{1}{x^2}\sin\frac{1}{x}\,dx = -\int \sin t\,dt = \cos t = \cos\frac{1}{x}\). Hence \(\frac{y}{x^2} = \cos\frac{1}{x} + C\), and the general solution is \(y = x^2\left(\cos\frac{1}{x} + C\right)\).

rows.stem:
Find the particular solution of the differential equation :
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \sin(x + y) + \sin(x - y)\), given that when \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\), y = 0.
rows.solution: First combine the two sines using \(\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B) = 2\sin A\cos B\) with \(A = x\) and \(B = y\): the equation becomes \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2\sin x\cos y\). The variables now separate: \(\frac{dy}{\cos y} = 2\sin x\,dx\), that is \(\sec y\,dy = 2\sin x\,dx\). Integrating both sides, and using \(\int \sec y\,dy = \log|\sec y + \tan y|\) and \(\int 2\sin x\,dx = -2\cos x\), gives \(\log|\sec y + \tan y| = -2\cos x + C\). Apply the given condition \(y = 0\) when \(x = \frac{\pi}{4}\): the left side is \(\log|1 + 0| = 0\), and the right side is \(-2\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + C = -\sqrt{2} + C\), so \(C = \sqrt{2}\). The particular solution is \(\log|\sec y + \tan y| = -2\cos x + \sqrt{2}\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following linear programming problem graphically :
Maximize z = 600x + 400y
subject to the constraints :
\(x + 2y \le 12\),
\(2x + y \le 12\),
\(x + 1{\cdot}25y \ge 5\),
\(x, y \ge 0\)
rows.solution: Treat each constraint as a boundary line and find where they meet. The line \(x + 1{\cdot}25y = 5\) cuts the axes at \((0, 4)\) and \((5, 0)\); \(x + 2y = 12\) cuts the y-axis at \((0, 6)\); \(2x + y = 12\) cuts the x-axis at \((6, 0)\); and solving \(x + 2y = 12\) with \(2x + y = 12\) simultaneously gives \(x = y = 4\), the point \((4, 4)\). Since \(x + 1{\cdot}25y \ge 5\) excludes the corner at the origin, the feasible region is the bounded five-sided region with corner points \((0, 4)\), \((0, 6)\), \((4, 4)\), \((6, 0)\) and \((5, 0)\). Evaluating \(z = 600x + 400y\) at each: \(z(0, 4) = 1600\), \(z(0, 6) = 2400\), \(z(4, 4) = 2400 + 1600 = 4000\), \(z(6, 0) = 3600\), \(z(5, 0) = 3000\). The region is bounded, so the greatest of these is the maximum: \(z = 4000\), attained at \(x = 4\), \(y = 4\).

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the lines y = 4x + 5, x + y = 5 and 4y = x + 5, using integration.
rows.solution: First find the vertices of the triangle by intersecting the lines in pairs. Solving \(y = 4x + 5\) with \(x + y = 5\) gives \(5x = 0\), so \(A(0, 5)\). Solving \(y = 4x + 5\) with \(4y = x + 5\) gives \(16x + 20 = x + 5\), so \(x = -1\) and \(B(-1, 1)\). Solving \(x + y = 5\) with \(4y = x + 5\) gives \(20 - 4x = x + 5\), so \(x = 3\) and \(C(3, 2)\). Across the whole span \(-1 \le x \le 3\) the lower boundary is the single line \(4y = x + 5\), i.e. \(y = \frac{x + 5}{4}\), which passes through both \(B\) and \(C\). The upper boundary changes at \(x = 0\): it is \(y = 4x + 5\) on \([-1, 0]\) and \(y = 5 - x\) on \([0, 3]\). Hence the area is \(\int_{-1}^{0}(4x + 5)\,dx + \int_{0}^{3}(5 - x)\,dx - \int_{-1}^{3}\frac{x + 5}{4}\,dx\). Evaluating each: \(\left[\frac{(4x + 5)^2}{8}\right]_{-1}^{0} = \frac{25}{8} - \frac{1}{8} = 3\); \(\left[\frac{(5 - x)^2}{-2}\right]_{0}^{3} = -2 + \frac{25}{2} = \frac{21}{2}\); and \(\left[\frac{(x + 5)^2}{8}\right]_{-1}^{3} = 8 - 2 = 6\). Therefore the area is \(3 + \frac{21}{2} - 6 = \frac{15}{2}\) square units.
